claims.statement: The same CodeActAgent, run with no modification to its system prompt across categories, is competitive with category-specialist and prior domain-general baselines on most of the 15 benchmarks tested, spanning software engineering, web browsing, and miscellaneous assistance.

datasets: the 11 benchmarks with confidently-recovered numbers, across all 3 categories
scope.conditions: one agent class, unmodified prompt, per-category delegation to BrowsingAgent/GPTSwarm where the paper itself uses it

confidence_reasons: directly stated by the authors (E110)
supported by measured claims in all 3 categories
counter-examples exist (C006, C010's code subset) and are folded into the claim's own scope ('most of')
no controlled single-variable ablation isolates the architecture's contribution from the backbone LLM's

claims.statement: Within the same agent scaffold, benchmark score scales strongly with backbone-LLM capability -- e.g. MINT math/code rise from 33.8%/5.2% (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) to 77.3%/50.0% (gpt-4o), and AgentBench-OS rises from 11.8% to 57.6% for the same model swap -- suggesting the residual gap to specialists tracks the backbone model at least as much as the platform's architecture.
confidence_reasons: the scaling pattern is consistent across three independent benchmark families
no controlled ablation isolates model capability from other confounds (e.g. training data recency)
single run per cell

claims.statement: The cross-category competitiveness pattern is not universal: on MiniWoB++ and the MINT code subset, OpenHands clearly trails a specialist or baseline system.
confidence_reasons: hard, unambiguous, directly observed in two independent benchmarks; no interpretive leap required

claims.statement: Software is one of the most powerful, general-purpose interfaces available for acting on the world, which motivates code execution as OpenHands' core interaction mechanism.
confidence_reasons: directly quotes the authors' own stated motivation

claims.statement: A shared, standardized tool library is motivated by the observation that a carefully crafted agent-computer interface matters, while building and maintaining one bespoke interface per agent implementation does not scale.
confidence_reasons: directly quotes the authors' own stated motivation, citing SWE-Agent's ACI finding

claims.statement: OpenHands chose a code-execution action space (bash, Python, browser) over fixed JSON tool-calling because it is a comprehensive, flexible, reliable, and easy-to-maintain set of primitives, while remaining compatible with tool-calling agents.
confidence_reasons: directly quotes the authors' own stated design rationale

claims.statement: OpenHands isolates every task session in its own Docker sandbox so that agent-driven code execution cannot damage the user's own system.
confidence_reasons: directly reflects the authors' own stated motivating question (safety) paired with their sandbox design

claims.statement: AgentSkills only adds a tool when the LLM cannot already write the needed code directly, or the tool must call an external model, to avoid re-teaching agents things they already know.
confidence_reasons: directly quotes the authors' own stated inclusion criterion

confidence_reasons: directly quotes the authors' own stated rationale

limitations.statement: Multi-modal file handling (images, video, office documents) is not yet integrated in a principled way through standard IPython/browser channels; current coverage comes only from predefined skills.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: bounds how general the 'general action space' claim is: general across bash/Python/browser text-based interaction, not yet across arbitrary modalities.
limitations.resolution: authors name this as future work (N31).

limitations.statement: Current agents, OpenHands' own included, still struggle with complex tasks.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: this is the broad, central boundary on the cross-category competitiveness finding: 'competitive' is relative to the baselines shown, not a claim of reliable, general task competence.
limitations.resolution: authors name training- and inference-time improvements as future work (N29).

limitations.statement: The current agent performs poorly when editing long files.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: bounds the practical reliability of the code-execution action space specifically for large-file editing tasks.
limitations.resolution: authors name file-editing improvements as future work.

limitations.statement: The HumanEvalFix comparison against SWE-Agent's 87.7% is not a matched comparison: SWE-Agent was given a full 1-shot demonstration trajectory, while OpenHands was evaluated 0-shot.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: the one benchmark row where a compared agent exceeds OpenHands by a wide margin is explained by an experimental-condition difference the authors themselves flag, not by a clean architectural shortfall -- but it also means the 79.3% vs. 87.7% comparison cannot be read as apples-to-apples evidence either way.

limitations.statement: OpenHands' own agent workflows still require substantial handcrafted engineering; automatic workflow generation is future work.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: qualifies how much of the platform's capability is 'built-in' versus requiring manual engineering per new agent/workflow.
limitations.resolution: authors point to graph-based frameworks (GPTSwarm, LangGraph) as candidate solutions (N30).

limitations.statement: Additional caveats. Baselines across the 15 benchmarks differ in backbone LLM, shot count, and training regime (zero/few-shot prompted vs. fine-tuned vs. RL-trained specialist), so the cross-category pattern reflects the platform-plus-backbone combination as evaluated, not a controlled, single-variable ablation of the architecture's own contribution.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: limits how much of the 'competitive across categories' finding can be attributed to the platform's design, as opposed to the choice of backbone LLM or the specific baselines each benchmark's own authors happened to compare against.
limitations.resolution: none available from this evidence; noted as a caveat on interpretation, not resolved.

limitations.statement: Additional caveats. Every benchmark cell in the evidence is a single run; no seed or trial variance is reported anywhere in the extracted tables.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: the exact size of any single-point gap (e.g. GPQA's 52.0% vs. 38.8%, or Entity Deduction Arena's 38.0% vs. 40.0%) should be read as a point estimate whose sensitivity to reruns cannot be assessed from this evidence.
limitations.resolution: none available from this evidence; noted as a caveat on interpretation, not resolved.

limitations.statement: Additional caveats. The competitiveness pattern is not universal: MiniWoB++ and the MINT code subset are counter-examples where OpenHands clearly trails a specialist or baseline system, so 'competitive across categories' should be read as a typical/aggregate pattern rather than uniform parity or superiority on every one of the 15 benchmarks.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: prevents over-reading the central finding as universal; it is a majority pattern with visible exceptions.
limitations.resolution: none needed; this caveat is itself the resolution (scope the central claim to 'most of').
